title: Hampshire College Summer Studies in Mathematics (HCSSiM)
description: A six-week residential summer program in college-level mathematics for talented, highly motivated high school students, held on the Hampshire College campus in Amherst, Massachusetts since 1971. Students spend four hours in morning classes six days a week (Monday-Saturday), followed by a pre-supper 'Prime Time Theorem' session and evening problem sessions, with afternoons left for rest, recreation, and informal study. The curriculum explores active, applicable areas of mathematics such as graph theory, dynamical systems, knot theory, and cryptography through a discovery-based approach emphasizing proof, modeling, and collaborative problem-solving over rote instruction. Teaching is done by faculty together with a tiered staff of graduate and undergraduate junior staff, who teach several hours per week and, by the end of the summer, design and lead their own mini-courses.
selectivity_evidence: Official site states the program receives 'way too many strong applications' each year; admission requires a math 'sponsor' recommendation letter, a personal essay, and passing a timed take-home 'Interesting Test' of challenging problems sent to applicants in March.

title: MIT PRIMES
description: A year-long, mentored mathematics and computer science research program run by the MIT Mathematics Department. The flagship MIT PRIMES track serves sophomores and juniors who live within commuting distance of Boston and meet weekly in person with a mentor - typically an MIT graduate student or postdoctoral researcher working under an MIT faculty member - on an open research problem in pure or applied math, theoretical computer science, or computational biology; a parallel PRIMES-USA track offers the same style of distance-mentored research to students across the rest of the United States. The program runs in four phases across the year: an advanced reading period (January-March), active research with weekly mentor meetings (March-June), independent study over the summer with email contact (June-August), and project write-up and presentation (September-December). Students must commit at least 10 hours per week during active research phases; the program states it admits only a small number of candidates with an advanced math background and extraordinary mathematical ability.
citizenship_restrictions: PRIMES is available only to students who reside in the United States.
residency_restrictions: The flagship MIT PRIMES track requires living within commuting distance of Boston; PRIMES-USA serves students residing elsewhere in the United States via distance mentoring.
selectivity_evidence: Official program materials state that PRIMES 'admits a small number of candidates' each year and expects applicants to have 'a very advanced background,' having 'demonstrated extraordinary mathematical ability and potential for conducting original research'; competitive preferred qualifications include being a USAMO/USAJMO qualifier or having earned an A in a college-level proof-based math course.

title: MITES Summer
description: A six-week residential STEM enrichment program at MIT for rising high school seniors, historically known as MIT Introduction to Technology, Engineering, and Science and now offered as one of three MITES tracks (alongside MITES Semester and MITES Saturdays). Students live on the MIT campus and take a full course load of college-level science, engineering, and math classes taught by MIT-affiliated instructors, building both academic skill and confidence for students - primarily from underrepresented and underserved backgrounds - considering STEM study and careers. All tuition, housing, and meal costs are fully covered by MIT and its funders; students are responsible only for their own transportation to and from campus, and travel scholarships are available. Admission is holistic, weighing demonstrated STEM interest and academic performance rather than a minimum GPA cutoff.
selectivity_evidence: MITES Summer's own FAQ describes a holistic, competitive selection process (short-answer essays and teacher recommendations submitted via an application portal) for a small, fully-funded residential cohort restricted to rising high school seniors nationally; the official site states admission 'is holistic' with no GPA cutoff, weighing demonstrated STEM interest and preparation instead.

title: Simons Summer Research Program
description: A seven-week, in-person research apprenticeship at Stony Brook University for rising high school seniors, running since 1984. Each accepted student (a 'Simons Fellow') is individually matched with a Stony Brook faculty mentor in a specific science, math, or engineering research group based on the student's top three preferred research areas, and works alongside that group learning laboratory techniques and research methods as a genuine team member. The program concludes with each Fellow producing a written research abstract and presenting a research poster summarizing their project. There is no academic tuition or program fee, but participants are responsible for their own commuting or on-campus housing/dining costs.
selectivity_evidence: Official application guidelines state the program's acceptance rate is approximately less than 5%, noting it 'receives far more applications from qualified students than can be accommodated'; the process requires a school-official nomination, two teacher recommendation letters, an unofficial transcript, and short essay responses, restricted to current 11th-graders at least 16 years old.

title: Garcia Summer Research Program
organization: Stony Brook University (Garcia Center for Polymers at Engineered Interfaces)
description: A seven-week, in-person research program at Stony Brook University's Garcia Center for Polymers at Engineered Interfaces, run in separate tracks for high school students, undergraduates, and teachers. High-school participants combine formal instruction with an independent, original research project designed with guidance from Garcia Center faculty, staff, and graduate students, working alongside undergraduates, teachers, and postdocs in shared research teams; research areas include polymer blends and composites, polymer/inorganic surfaces, protein and DNA interactions, polymer recycling, materials engineering, and related theoretical modeling and analytical techniques such as x-ray/neutron scattering, microscopy, and spectroscopy. Participants who complete a successful project may go on to publish in a research journal or present at a professional conference such as the Materials Research Society Fall Meeting, and high-school Scholars can continue afterward in an optional year-round mentor program.
citizenship_restrictions: International students may apply only if they already hold legal documentation to be in the U.S. during the program; the center does not sponsor visas.
selectivity_evidence: Official eligibility requirements set explicit minimum bars for high-school applicants: unweighted GPA of at least 95/100 (3.8/4.0), standardized test scores (PSAT/SAT/ACT/AP/IB/Regents) at or above the 60th percentile, and completion of at least three specified science/math courses (honors or AP/IB preferred); the official page also notes that leadership and extracurricular involvement receive 'preferential evaluation' in a competitive review.

title: Anson L. Clark Scholars Program
description: A seven-week, in-person summer research program at Texas Tech University for twelve rising high school seniors or recent graduates selected nationally, running for more than 30 years and funded by an endowment from the Anson L. Clark Foundation. Unlike most STEM-only research programs, Clark Scholars are drawn from 'almost any area of academe' - natural sciences, mathematics, humanities, and fine arts alike - and each is individually paired with a Texas Tech faculty mentor (on the main campus or the Health Sciences Center) for hands-on, one-on-one original research. Alongside their individual research, Scholars attend weekly seminars, group discussions, and field trips, and each completes the program by producing a formal written research report, for which they receive a $750 stipend upon successful completion.
selectivity_evidence: The program selects just twelve Scholars nationally each year ('twelve highly qualified rising high school seniors and recent high school graduates'); official application requirements include SAT/ACT (or PSAT/PACT) scores, a high school transcript, three letters of recommendation, multiple short essays, and a ranked list of top activities, reviewed competitively for a fixed cohort of 12.

title: JAX Summer Student Program
description: A fully funded, ten-week residential research fellowship in mammalian genetics and genomics at The Jackson Laboratory, open to graduating high school seniors and undergraduates and offered at two sites: Bar Harbor, Maine, and The Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine in Farmington, Connecticut. Each student joins an active JAX lab as a mentored researcher working on a genetics/genomics project alongside JAX faculty, trainees, and staff, and supplements the lab work with co-curricular training in scientific communication, professional development, and responsible conduct of research, plus weekly Journal Club meetings and conversations with JAX scientists across different career paths. All students receive a $7,500 stipend for the ten weeks, along with fully covered room, board, and round-trip travel between home and the Laboratory.
selectivity_evidence: Official admissions page states admission to the Summer Student Program 'is competitive'; the program is a fully funded research fellowship (housing, meals, a $7,500 stipend, and covered travel) open to graduating high school seniors and undergraduates, requiring a full application with standard personal and academic materials per the official checklist.

title: Canada/USA Mathcamp
description: A five-week residential summer program in advanced mathematics for mathematically talented students ages 13-18 from around the world, run at a different host college campus each summer (Champlain College in Burlington, Vermont, in 2026) since 1993. Mathcamp has no fixed curriculum or requirements; instead, faculty and visiting speakers teach courses (ranging from a few days to five weeks long) on advanced and unusual pure and applied math topics of their own choosing, and each of the roughly 120 campers per summer (a mix of new and returning students) works with an academic advisor to build a personalized schedule drawn from these classes, problem-solving sessions, hands-on workshops, individual projects, unstructured 'TAU' study time, and colloquia by visiting mathematicians. Admission is based on the 'Qualifying Quiz,' described as the centerpiece of the application: 5-10 challenging problems that assume only standard high-school math background but require deep, original mathematical thinking.
selectivity_evidence: Admission is centered on a required 'Qualifying Quiz' of 5-10 original, challenging problems that the official site calls 'the centerpiece of the Mathcamp application'; the official Fast Facts page states total annual enrollment is only about 120 students (mixing incoming and returning campers) with a 4:1 student-to-staff ratio, drawn from an international applicant pool. Admission is explicitly need-blind: financial aid applications are reviewed only after admission decisions are finalized.
